summary: Captures experience from implementing the ForCES protocol and model, in which a control element manages forwarding elements. It aims to help others with examples and possible implementation strategies. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two parts of a router, the brain and the muscles, can be separated and talk by messages. People who built it share tips and lessons so others have an easier time.

questions: forwarding and control element separation tips
subtitle: Lessons learned from building the ForCES protocol that separates a router's control and forwarding planes.

tldr.problem: ForCES is a complex protocol for separating a router's brain (control element) from its muscles (forwarding element), but implementation challenges were not yet documented.
tldr.mechanism: Three researchers who built ForCES implementations describe the architecture, model design patterns, protocol handling strategies, and practical choices they made. They cover components, logical functional blocks (LFBs), message deserialization and serialization, and development platform considerations.
tldr.outcome: Implementers gain concrete strategies for building their own ForCES systems, including object-oriented design patterns, recursive TLV handling, and SCTP/IPsec deployment considerations.

facts.label: Interoperability tests
facts.value: Two successful tests; tested across Greece-China distance

today: RFC 6369 is an Informational RFC that captures lessons learned by ForCES implementers. It remains a key reference for anyone building ForCES systems, offering design patterns and strategies proven in practice.

sections.title: Introduction to ForCES Architecture
sections.content:
The Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) protocol lets a Control Element (CE) manage one or more Forwarding Elements (FEs). The FE handles packet processing under CE direction. The protocol uses Logical Functional Blocks (LFBs) as the basic abstraction, where each LFB is a configurable piece of the FE's functionality.

The Transport Mapping Layer (TML) carries ForCES protocol messages. While other TMPs may exist, all implementations must support SCTP TML with IPsec for security. The document captures implementation experience and alternatives from two successful ForCES interoperability tests.
sections.eli5: The protocol lets a brain (control element) send instructions to muscles (forwarding element) on how to handle network traffic. This document shares tips from people who built it.

sections.title: Model Design and Components
sections.content:
The ForCES model is dynamic: developers define custom components (operational parameters) and LFBs (logical functional blocks) by inheriting from base data types. The key insight is building a scalable architecture where new LFBs and components reuse existing code.

The authors recommend creating a base component class with fields like component ID, access rights, min/max size, and whether it is optional or variable-sized. Basic functions include Get/Set/Delete operations for full data, sparse data, and properties. Atomic data types form the foundation, then compound types (structs and arrays) inherit and specialize them. For arrays, a mother component can spawn new rows when Set commands arrive.

For LFBs, use the same inheritance pattern: a parent LFB class has class ID, instance ID, component arrays, capabilities, and events. Each specific LFB inherits and adds its own components. This approach allows one developer to write LFB handling logic once, then reuse it for all LFBs.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing code for every piece of the router from scratch, you build base blocks and let new pieces inherit from them. It is like building with Lego blocks instead of starting from raw plastic each time.

sections.title: Protocol Message Handling
sections.content:
ForCES messages consist of a common header followed by Type-Length-Value (TLV) units. The TLV hierarchy has multiple levels: LFBselect-TLVs at the top, OPER-TLVs for operations, PATH-DATA-TLVs for addressing components, and leaf TLVs like FULLDATA-TLV, SPARSEDATA-TLV, and RESULT-TLV.

Message deserialization requires reading the header, determining message type, and recursively parsing nested TLVs. When a PATH-DATA-TLV contains another PATH-DATA-TLV, recursion handles the nesting until reaching a leaf TLV. All TLVs must be 32-bit aligned; the length field includes Type and Length (4 bytes) but not padding.

For serialization, build TLVs bottom-up: create leaf TLVs, wrap them in OPER-TLVs, those in LFBselect-TLVs, and finally insert into the common header. This modular approach lets developers create any message type dynamically.
sections.eli5: Messages are like Russian nesting dolls. You read the outer doll, see what is inside, then open that to see what is in it, and so on. Writing messages is the reverse: you build the smallest piece, wrap it in a bigger piece, and keep wrapping.

sections.title: Deployment and Development Platforms
sections.content:
All ForCES implementations must support SCTP as the Transport Mapping Layer. Developers must use IPsec for security. The implementations have been tested remotely across networks; one interoperability test connected systems between Greece and China successfully. However, if FE and CE are behind NAT or firewalls, SCTP ports must be forwarded and firewall rules must allow SCTP.

Development platforms include Windows, Linux, and Solaris for C/C++. Java support is more limited. A key challenge for Java developers is that Java lacks unsigned integer types; a workaround is to create wrapper classes that translate unsigned types to signed Java types.
sections.eli5: You can build this on Windows, Linux, or Solaris using C, C++, or Java. If the routers are on different networks, make sure firewalls do not block the communication between them.

sections.title: Security and Best Practices
sections.content:
Implementers must follow the security considerations in the ForCES framework and protocol specifications. Transport-level security is mandatory: IPsec must protect SCTP connections. Initial configuration of FE and CE is handled by FE Manager and CE Manager entities (not yet standardized); the simplest approach is static configuration files. For more dynamic setups, managers exchange identifiers, IP addresses, TML type, and priority ports.

The authors note that ForCES was designed for local deployment but has proven deployable remotely when proper network configuration is in place. Strong cryptography and valid certificates are essential.
sections.eli5: Protect messages with strong encryption. Set up the brain and muscles ahead of time with configuration files or a management tool. You can run them on different networks, but security is mandatory.
